children: By Philip van Doorn
Chemical company Mosaic's stock is the strongest performer among the S&P 500, while several tech players and associated power providers show sharp declines
Investors gave a nod of approval, sending all the broad U.S. stock indexes up significantly after the Democratic Party won control of both houses of Congress.
(Updated with closing prices on Nov. 4.)
The broad stock indexes roared on Wednesday following an overwhelming set of election victories for the Democratic Party, which won majorities in both houses of Congress.
Given that affordability was a key issue for voters, some of the biggest beneficiaries of the election's results were shares of companies in the home-building, retail and healthcare industries.
Meanwhile, some of the biggest decliners were shares of companies that would be hurt by the Democrats' push to slow the build-out of artificial-intelligence infrastructure, such as data centers.
The S&P 500 SPX rose 1.6% on Wednesday, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA soared 1,569 points, or 3%, to close at 53,356.12. The Nasdaq Composite Index (COMP) rose 1.4%.

Another notable development was that the S&P 500 home-building industry group was up 7.3% for the session, according to FactSet.

Mosaic (MOS) led the S&P 500 on Wednesday with a gain of 17.3%, after the supplier of phosphate and potash reported a third-quarter net loss of $72 million, compared with a net loss of $273 million in the second quarter and a profit of $411 million in the third quarter of 2025. Third-quarter net sales came in at $3.1 billion, compared with $2.8 billion the previous quarter and $3.5 billion in the year-earlier quarter.

Mosaic CEO Bruce Bodine said in the earnings release that the company "continued to advance opportunities to optimize the portfolio" amid supply challenges, for better positioning when industry conditions improve. The company also said it expected to reduce its capital expenditures to $1 billion in 2027 from an estimated total of $1.2 billion this year.

Block (XYZ) was next with a 15.4% gain, after the payment processor provided a preliminary 2027 outlook calling for a 5% increase in revenue and a 30% increase in earnings, matching the current full-year outlook for 2026.

Stanley Black & Decker (SWK) rose 13.2% after the company reported a vastly improved profit margin and an increase in third-quarter net earnings to $272.1 million from $51.4 million for the year-earlier quarter. The toolmaker also increased its guidance range for 2026 earnings per share to between $5.45 and $5.85 from its previous guidance of $4.60 to $5.45.

Fidelity National Information Services (FIS) was the worst performer among the S&P 500 on Wednesday, with shares of the financial industry service provider falling 23.5%.

Early on Wednesday, the company lowered its outlook for sales and earnings for 2026 and initiated guidance for 2027 that disappointed investors. Oppenheimer analyst Rayna Kumar downgraded the stock to perform from outperform, writing in a note to clients that systems-conversion delays for new customers, as well as "bank consolidation, lower license and termination fees, and higher tax and interest expense," all weighed on Fidelity National's 2027 outlook.
